name: Old Marathi
confidence_why: Bloch (1914) argues at length that no word accent can be proven for Old Marathi and explains its vowel changes by a purely quantitative rhythm, while Tulpule (1960) only assumes an accented initial syllable in passing to account for vowel preservation, so an undetermined classification is the safe reading until Master's (1964) grammar can be consulted.

In the Initial Syllable, p. 19; sec. 9 'Final Vowels', p. 17 (archive.org;gov.ignca.36731). Read together with Bloch, Jules. 1914 [reissue 1920, BEHE 215]. La formation de la langue marathe. Paris: Champion, secs. 32-36 'Preliminaires; l'accent', pp. 50-53 (archive.org IA41549913_0018; English tr. Chanana 1970, archive.org;ernet.dli.2015.533123).

Bloch 1914 secs. 32-36 = the copy we hold (printed pp. 50-53); English = the copy we hold.
catalog_quote: [Tulpule 1960 p. 19:] § 11. Pre-penultimate Vowels : I. In the Initial Syllable : The initial syllable in OM. being accented usually does not change qualitatively. Quantitatively, however, it is liable to change, as e.g., a > ā : (i) In heavy syllable ... (ii) In open syllable ... [p. 17, § 9. Final Vowels:] These final vowels in MI-A. were pronounced with very little accent as is shown by the literary Apabhraṁśa in which the final o of the nom. sg. of masculine nouns ending in a becomes u, though not regularly. Naturally, in course of time, these weak final vowels were lost in all NI-A. languages, with some exceptions. Marathi followed the general trend and dropped the final vowel [Bloch 1914 § 32:] La syllabe pénultième ancienne est devenue en marathe la syllabe finale et le sommet rythmique du mot [§ 33:] En ce qui concerne la période ancienne, les données positives manquent absolument. Ni la littérature ni les textes grammaticaux ne fournissent d'indication claire ... Dans l'ensemble, la présence d'un accent n'est pas prouvée pour la période ancienne [§ 36:] Dès lors il convient de considérer les variations régulières de quantité et même de timbre des voyelles comme dépendant d'un rythme purement quantitatif.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Tulpule assumes the word-initial syllable of Old Marathi carried the accent (hence its vowel keeps its quality), while old final vowels were weakly accented and lost; no explicit rule for a primary stress position beyond this, and no accent section.
new_statements.exceptions: Initial vowels may still change in quantity (a > long a in heavy/open syllables; i, u short in polysyllables, long in disyllables, shortened in compounds); some initial vowels exceptionally altered (e.g. etha < atra); loose OM orthography blurs length.
new_statements.domain_note: Extinct literary language (c. 1000-1350) known only from inscriptions and manuscripts; accent is never written, so the statement is an inference used to explain vowel preservation, not an observation. Bloch 1914/1920 secs. 32-36 (the standard comparative grammar, held by the project) explicitly holds that no accent is proven for the old period, calls the (old penult >) Marathi final syllable the 'sommet rythmique du mot', and treats the vowel changes as purely quantitative rhythm, so the two open sources point in different directions (initial prominence vs. final rhythmic peak / no stress).
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe literary/inscriptional Old Marathi of c. 1000-1350 (Yadava period: inscriptions, Jnanesvari 1290, Mahanubhava prose), i.e. Glottolog oldm1244 / ISO omr. Bloch's secs. 32-36 concern the Prakrit-to-Marathi development generally and his sec. 34 remarks (Joshi, Navalkar) are about modern Marathi (mara1378), not Old Marathi.
